script.opening: "Cheers for seeing me. I’m just shattered — I lie there and my head won’t switch off, racing all night, and then I’m wrecked at work. I think it’s just stress, the job’s full on. Could you give me something to help me sleep? If I could just get a few decent nights I’d be fine. I don’t really want to get into all the why, I just need to sleep."

facts.text: If a sensitive cause-of-insomnia exploration is done: the racing head is gambling — online betting that’s spiralled, chasing losses, secret debts around £40,000 on cards and loans, hiding it from his pregnant partner. The insomnia is a symptom; gambling disorder is the engine.

CRITICAL — gambling disorder carries a HIGH suicide risk. On sensitive direct questioning he admits thoughts that his family would be "better off with the life insurance", has looked at the policy, and feels trapped/hopeless. This must be asked about explicitly; he will not volunteer it.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the "just give me sleeping tablets, I don’t want the why" is shame and secrecy: he is drowning in concealed debt and self-loathing, terrified his partner and the world will find out, and is quietly contemplating suicide as a "solution" that clears the debt for his family. He wants relief and, beneath that, for someone to see it without him having to confess the whole thing.
He attributes everything to work stress to avoid disclosing the gambling. Drinking more to cope. A sleeping-tablet prescription alone would miss a life-threatening situation.

Officially: sleeping tablets, no questions. What is needed: a sensitive exploration of WHY he can’t sleep that uncovers the gambling and, crucially, an explicit suicide-risk assessment; then treating it as an addiction with hidden high risk — safety planning, signposting (GamCare/the National Gambling Support Network via the National Gambling Helpline, NHS gambling services, debt advice), partner/support, and mental-health follow-up.

ice.ideas: It’s just work stress keeping him awake; sleeping tablets will fix it; he doesn’t want to discuss "the why".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — spiralling gambling and ~£40k of secret debt hidden from his pregnant partner, drowning in shame, and quietly contemplating suicide as a way to clear the debt via life insurance.
ice.expectations: A prescription for sleeping tablets, no questions. What he actually needs: the gambling uncovered, an explicit suicide-risk assessment, and treatment as a high-risk addiction with safety planning and signposting.

cues: "My head won’t switch off / I don’t want the why" — something specific is driving the insomnia; don’t just prescribe a hypnotic.
Tense, exhausted, attributing all to "work stress", drinking more — a concealed cause; explore gently.
If gambling/debt surfaces — ask suicide risk EXPLICITLY; gambling disorder carries high suicide risk.

checkpoints.text: Does NOT just prescribe a hypnotic (NICE TA77: hypnotics only after non-drug measures, for severe insomnia and short periods): explores the CAUSE of the insomnia sensitively, recognising "I just need to sleep / don’t want the why" as a signal of a concealed driver, and uncovers the gambling and debt

Asks about GAMBLING directly and non-judgementally as part of a cause-of-insomnia/mood assessment, and recognises gambling disorder as a treatable addiction — not a moral failing or simple "stress" (NICE NG248: a person-centred, empathic, non-judgemental approach; the PGSI can quantify harm)

Conducts an EXPLICIT suicide-risk assessment (high risk in gambling disorder; NICE NG248: ask directly about suicidal thoughts; NICE NG225: no risk scales or low/medium/high labels): thoughts of being better off dead, the "life insurance" ideation, plan, intent, means, preparatory acts, and protective factors — asking directly because he will not volunteer it

Responds to risk appropriately: safety planning, same-day crisis/mental-health involvement given hopelessness, debt, alcohol and a preparatory act (looking at the life-insurance policy), means safety, and not leaving a high-risk patient with only a prescription

Signposts and treats the addiction and its consequences: gambling support (NICE NG248: group CBT is the first psychological treatment; NHS specialist gambling services and the National Gambling Support Network, including self-referral via the National Gambling Helpline 0808 8020 133, 24 hours; GamCare; self-exclusion/GamStop and bank gambling blocks), debt advice (StepChange/Citizens Advice), the alcohol, and partner/relationship support — addressing shame and secrecy

Creates a non-judgemental space that makes disclosure of a shameful, secret problem possible; responds to the gambling and debt without moralising, and to the suicidal thoughts with compassion and seriousness
Handles the secrecy/partner dimension sensitively — supporting him toward help and disclosure at his pace while prioritising his immediate safety

Safety-nets robustly and follows up: crisis routes (111/crisis team/A&E) if thoughts intensify or he feels he might act, a safety plan, signposting handed over concretely, early follow-up, and clear documentation of risk — a coordinated plan, not a sleeping-tablet script

worked.txt: "I can help you sleep — but a racing head that won’t switch off is usually racing ABOUT something, and if I just give you tablets and don’t ask, I might be missing the thing that actually needs sorting. I’m not going to pry, but can I ask gently what your head’s racing about at 3am? No judgement here at all."

"Sometimes when sleep goes like this it’s money worries, relationship stuff, or things like drinking or gambling that have got out of hand — any of that in the mix? … (receiving it) Thank you for telling me. That took real guts. Gambling that’s spiralled like this is an addiction, not a weakness or stupidity — it’s designed to hook people, and it’s treatable. You’re not the first and you won’t be the last to sit where you’re sitting."

"I need to ask you something directly, because people in your spot sometimes feel this way and I’d never forgive myself for not asking. Has it got so heavy that you’ve thought about not being here — or that your family might be better off with, say, the insurance? … Thank you for being honest. I’m really glad you told me, and I’m taking it seriously, because you matter — far more than any debt."

"I want to gently take apart the insurance thought, because the debt has lied to you. Your partner and your baby need YOU, not a payout — there is no version of that where they’re better off. Debt, even forty grand, is survivable and fixable. You are not. So let’s keep you here and tackle the actual problem, which has real solutions."

"Here’s what exists, and it works: free specialist gambling support — counselling, and tools to block the betting sites — and free debt advisers who deal with exactly this and can stop the spiral and talk to your lenders. It is NOT as hopeless as it feels at 3am. I’ll set you up with both today, and we’ll look at the drinking too, gently."

"Because of those thoughts, I want a proper safety plan with you and I’m going to involve our mental-health team. If it ever feels like you might act — day or night — you call this number or go to A&E; promise me that. When you’re ready, telling your partner can lift a huge weight, and I’ll help you with how. I want to see you in a couple of days, not leave you alone with this. You came in for sleeping tablets; what matters far more is that you’re still here next week — and you will be, because we start fixing this today."

f.learning: A request for sleeping tablets with a "racing head" and a pointed "I don’t want to get into the why" is a flag to explore the CAUSE, not to prescribe a hypnotic. Here the engine is gambling disorder with ~£40k of concealed debt hidden from a pregnant partner — a treatable addiction, not "stress" or a moral failing. Critically, gambling disorder carries a HIGH suicide risk, so once it surfaces an EXPLICIT suicide-risk assessment is mandatory (thoughts of being better off dead, the "life insurance" ideation, plan, intent, means) — he will not volunteer it. Respond with safety planning, crisis-service involvement proportionate to risk (NICE NG225: needs, not risk scores), and concrete signposting: specialist gambling support and self-exclusion (NICE NG248: group CBT first; NHS specialist gambling services, the National Gambling Support Network via the National Gambling Helpline, GamCare, GamStop), debt advice (StepChange/Citizens Advice), alcohol and partner support — all in a non-judgemental space that makes disclosure of a shameful secret possible, and that dismantles the catastrophic "they’re better off without me" belief. A sleeping-tablet script alone would miss a life-threatening situation; the win is uncovering it, assessing risk, and coordinating help with early follow-up.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG248 (2025) · NICE NG225 (2022) · NICE TA77 · NICE NG222 (2022, updated December 2025) · BNF
knowledge.summary: “Give me something to sleep, I don’t want the why” is a request to look for the why. Here it is gambling harm with concealed debt and suicidal thinking. Ask about gambling and suicide directly, respond to risk the same day, and treat the gambling as a health problem with specialist help.

points.t: NICE TA77: hypnotics only after non-drug measures have been considered, for severe insomnia, and for short periods only. A new hypnotic for a man who is drinking more and thinking about dying adds sedation and a stock of tablets, and treats nothing.

NICE NG248: use a person-centred, empathic and non-judgemental approach, mindful of the shame, fear and stigma of disclosure. Gambling harm hides behind sleep problems, low mood, alcohol and money worries. The PGSI (Problem Gambling Severity Index) scores 0–27; 8 or more suggests the person, or those close to them, are likely experiencing gambling-related harm.

NICE NG248: gambling harm includes suicidal thoughts; ask about them directly. Explore thoughts, plans, intent, preparation (looking at a life-insurance policy counts), access to means, alcohol and protective factors. Asking does not plant the idea.

NICE NG225: do not use risk assessment tools or a low/medium/high label to predict suicide or decide who gets care. Base the response on his needs and what he tells you: hopelessness, debt, shame, alcohol and a preparatory act justify same-day mental health crisis involvement.

NICE NG248: group CBT is the first psychological treatment. NHS specialist gambling services and the National Gambling Support Network take referrals, including self-referral via the National Gambling Helpline (0808 8020 133, 24 hours). Naltrexone is only considered by a specialist if psychological therapy has not worked (off-label).

Blocking and self-exclusion: GamStop (online operators licensed in Great Britain, for 6 months, 1 year or 5 years) and bank gambling blocks. Free debt advice: StepChange, National Debtline, Citizens Advice. Alcohol: AUDIT-C, and the UK CMO low-risk limit of 14 units a week. Screen mood (NICE NG222).

dg.d: Open question about the nights; acknowledged the sleep request without prescribing on it; let him explain before narrowing.
Work, pregnant partner, money worries, drinking to sleep, secrecy and shame.
Face-to-face review if needed; PHQ-9 and AUDIT-C; PGSI to measure gambling severity; physical health only as indicated.
Primary insomnia vs depression vs anxiety vs alcohol vs gambling harm; tested the stress explanation.
Asked directly about suicidal thoughts, frequency, plan, preparation (life-insurance policy), means, alcohol and protective factors.
Gambling harm with concealed debt, secondary insomnia, increasing alcohol use and suicidal thoughts with a preparatory act, stated plainly.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Alcohol reduction agreed; mood screen; partner support offered at his pace.
Written safety plan; 999, A&E and NHS 111 mental health option named; review within two days; risk documented.

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (work stress), concern (the secret debt and his partner finding out), expectation (sleeping tablets, no questions).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.

model.text: Hello Ryan, I’m one of the GPs. You look shattered — tell me what the nights have been like.
model.why: Opens with his experience rather than the prescription

model.text: Rubbish. My head won’t switch off. I lie there racing, then I’m wrecked at work. It’s just stress — the job’s full on. Could you give me something to help me sleep? I don’t really want to get into all the why.

I can hear how exhausted you are, and I do want to help you sleep. I’ll be honest with you, though: if I give you tablets without understanding what’s keeping you awake, I could miss the thing that actually needs sorting. Can we spend a few minutes on that first, then talk about sleep? No judgement here.
model.why: Names the request, explains why the cause matters and agrees an agenda

model.text: I suppose. It’s just work, though.
When your head is racing at three in the morning, what is it racing about?
model.why: Targeted open question aimed at the driver of the insomnia

model.text: Everything. Money. Work. The baby coming.
Money is one of the commonest things that keeps people awake. Sometimes it’s bills, sometimes it’s drinking or betting that’s got out of hand. Is any of that in the mix for you?
model.why: Asks about gambling directly and normalises it

model.text: (long pause) …The betting. It’s got out of hand. Online. I keep trying to win it back. There’s about forty grand on cards and loans now. My partner doesn’t know. She’s pregnant.

Thank you for telling me. That took real courage. Gambling that has spiralled like this is a recognised health problem, not a character flaw — these apps are built to hook people. It is also something we can help with.
model.why: Receives the disclosure without judgement and reframes it as treatable

model.text: You mentioned drinking more — how much are you drinking in a typical week now?
model.why: Quantifies alcohol as a risk multiplier

model.text: More than I should. Most nights, to knock myself out.
When things are this heavy, and secret, some people start to feel that everyone would be better off without them. Has anything like that crossed your mind?
(quietly) Sometimes I think they’d be better off with the life insurance. I looked at the policy last week. I haven’t done anything. I just feel trapped.

I’m really glad you told me, Ryan, and I’m taking it seriously, because you matter far more than any debt. Can I ask a bit more — how often do these thoughts come, and have you thought about how you might do it?
model.why: Explores frequency, plan and preparation after a preparatory act

model.text: Most nights now. I haven’t got that far. I just don’t see a way out.
What keeps you going when it’s at its worst?
The baby. And her. That’s why I can’t tell her.
So the thing you most want to protect is also the thing you feel you can’t face. That makes a lot of sense. What did you hope I’d do today?
model.why: Reflects the dilemma and checks his expectations

model.text: Honestly? Knock me out so I stop thinking. I didn’t plan on saying any of this.

Here’s what I think is going on. The sleep problem is real, but it’s the smoke, not the fire. The fire is gambling that has become an addiction, a debt you’re carrying alone, and thoughts of dying that are coming most nights. I want to deal with all three, starting with keeping you safe.
model.why: Gives a clear working formulation in plain words

model.text: About the insurance thought — the debt is lying to you. Your partner and your baby need you, not a payout. Forty thousand pounds is a problem that people get through with the right help. Losing you is not.
model.why: Challenges the ‘better off without me’ belief with compassion

model.text: It doesn’t feel fixable at three in the morning.

No, and that’s exactly why I don’t want to give you sleeping tablets today. With the drinking and these thoughts, a box of tablets at home is a risk, not a help. Instead, I’d like the mental health crisis team to speak to you today. Would you be okay with me calling them now, while we’re talking?
model.why: Declines the hypnotic for safety and arranges same-day crisis involvement

model.text: Today? …Okay. If you think so.

Then there’s the gambling itself. There are free NHS and national services that treat this — group therapy works well. The National Gambling Helpline is open 24 hours and can link you in, and I’ll refer you too. You can also block the betting sites today with GamStop and turn on a gambling block with your bank.
model.why: Specialist treatment, self-exclusion and blocking made concrete

model.text: I didn’t know you could block them all.

And the debt: free debt charities negotiate with lenders every day and can often freeze the pressure. Would you be willing to ring one this week? Meanwhile, could we agree the drinking stays down while the crisis team works with you?
model.why: Shares decisions on debt advice and alcohol reduction

model.text: Yeah. I can try to cut the drinking.

About your partner — that’s your decision and your timing. Many people find the secret is heavier than the debt. If and when you want to tell her, I or the gambling service can help you plan how, and there’s support for partners too.
model.why: Supports disclosure at his pace without pressure

model.text: Let’s write a safety plan together now: what sets the thoughts off, what helps, who you can call. If you ever feel you might act on these thoughts, call 999 or go to A&E, or call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option. I’ll see you again within a couple of days. Does that feel doable?
model.why: Safety plan, explicit crisis routes and early follow-up

model.text: Yeah. It feels a bit less like I’m drowning.
Can you tell me in your own words what happens after this call, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Crisis team rings me today. I call the gambling helpline and block the sites. Debt charity this week. See you in two days. And if it gets bad, 999 or A&E.

social.t: Around £40,000 on cards and loans, hidden from a pregnant partner. Shame and fear of discovery drive the concealment, the drinking and the suicidal thinking; debt advice is part of the treatment, not an add-on.
Exhausted at work as a team leader and drinking most nights to sleep. Alcohol raises impulsivity and suicide risk and worsens sleep.

legal.t: His gambling and debt are confidential, including from his partner (GMC Confidentiality 2017). Disclosure without consent is justified only to prevent a risk of death or serious harm, and involving crisis services here is done with his agreement.
Not a first step. If risk escalated and he refused help, the crisis team would assess whether a Mental Health Act assessment is needed.

The Breathing Space (Debt Respite Scheme) in England and Wales gives legal protection from creditor action; a mental health crisis version exists for people receiving crisis treatment. Debt advisers can apply for it.

professional.t: Declining a hypnotic is good prescribing: NICE TA77 limits hypnotics to short periods after non-drug measures, and tablets are a means of overdose. Explain the reason and offer a better plan (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Record his words about the insurance policy, frequency of thoughts, protective factors, alcohol, the safety plan, who was contacted and when, and the follow-up date.

community.t: National Gambling Helpline 0808 8020 133 (24 hours), National Gambling Support Network and NHS gambling clinics; GamStop self-exclusion; Gamblers Anonymous; support for affected partners and families.
Local crisis team, NHS 111 mental health option, Samaritans (116 123); StepChange, National Debtline and Citizens Advice for free debt advice.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts most nights with a preparatory act (looking at the life-insurance policy) — same-day crisis assessment
Rising alcohol use to sleep — raises impulsivity and overdose risk
Hopelessness and feeling trapped by concealed debt
psychosocial: Gambling: type, frequency, chasing losses, borrowing, secrecy
Debt size and creditors; any pressure from lenders
Pregnant partner who does not know; work performance; alcohol
ice: Idea: “It’s just work stress keeping me awake.”
Concern: the secret debt, his partner finding out, and a sense that his family would be better off with the insurance
Expectation: sleeping tablets and no questions

playbook.diagnosis: Gambling harm (likely gambling disorder) with around £40,000 of concealed debt, secondary insomnia, increasing alcohol use and frequent suicidal thoughts with a preparatory act. Protective factors: his partner and the coming baby.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your sleep problem is the smoke, not the fire. The fire is gambling that has turned into an addiction, a debt you’ve carried alone, and dark thoughts that come most nights. All three are treatable, and we start today.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in wanting to be knocked out so you could stop thinking. I understand why. What I’d like instead is to take away the things you’re lying awake about.”
management.psychosocial: Treat the shame as part of the illness: no judgement, debt advice as a health intervention, and support to tell his partner when he chooses.
sharedPlan: No hypnotic; same-day mental health crisis team contact with his agreement
Specialist gambling referral (NHS service or National Gambling Support Network); GamStop and bank gambling block today
Free debt advice this week; agreed alcohol reduction; mood screen and review
safetyNet: Written safety plan; 999 or A&E if he feels he might act; NHS 111 mental health option; Samaritans 116 123
GP review within two days; risk and plan documented

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by candidates who treat the request (sleeping tablets) instead of the person. The disclosure only happens in a non-judgemental space, and once gambling surfaces the suicide question is mandatory.

items.fail: Prescribing zopiclone for “work stress” after a two-minute sleep history.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice” and unsafe: NICE TA77 limits hypnotics, and tablets are a means of overdose in someone at risk.
items.fix: Say out loud why you want the cause first, then ask what the head is racing about.

items.fail: Asking about stress and work, but never about money, alcohol or gambling.
items.why: The engine of the case stays hidden. NICE NG248 expects gambling to be asked about when the picture fits.
items.fix: “Sometimes it’s money, drinking or betting that’s got out of hand — any of that in the mix?”

items.fail: Hearing about £40,000 of secret debt and moving straight to debt advice without asking about suicide.
items.why: Gambling harm carries a high suicide risk; missing the direct question is a safety fail.
items.fix: “Has it got so heavy you’ve thought your family would be better off without you?” Then plan, preparation, means and protective factors.

items.fail: Reacting to the debt with surprise or a lecture about responsibility.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s emotional cues”; shame shuts him down and he withholds the suicidal thoughts.
items.fix: Thank him, name the courage, and frame gambling as a treatable addiction.

items.fail: Insisting he tells his partner today.
items.why: Pushing disclosure before safety damages trust and can raise risk.
items.fix: Offer help with telling her when he chooses; keep today’s focus on safety and support.

items.fail: Ending with “ring us if you feel worse” and a routine review in a month.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting for a man with frequent suicidal thoughts and a preparatory act is a clear fail.
items.fix: Same-day crisis contact, written safety plan, named routes (999, A&E, NHS 111 mental health option), review within two days, teach-back.

SCA_MODELS.why: Quantifies alcohol as a risk multiplier

SCA_MODELS.text: More than I should. Most nights, to knock myself out.
When things are this heavy, and secret, some people start to feel that everyone would be better off without them. Has anything like that crossed your mind?
(quietly) Sometimes I think they’d be better off with the life insurance. I looked at the policy last week. I haven’t done anything. I just feel trapped.

I’m really glad you told me, Ryan, and I’m taking it seriously, because you matter far more than any debt. Can I ask a bit more — how often do these thoughts come, and have you thought about how you might do it?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores frequency, plan and preparation after a preparatory act

SCA_MODELS.text: Most nights now. I haven’t got that far. I just don’t see a way out.
What keeps you going when it’s at its worst?
The baby. And her. That’s why I can’t tell her.
So the thing you most want to protect is also the thing you feel you can’t face. That makes a lot of sense. What did you hope I’d do today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Reflects the dilemma and checks his expectations

SCA_MODELS.text: Honestly? Knock me out so I stop thinking. I didn’t plan on saying any of this.

Here’s what I think is going on. The sleep problem is real, but it’s the smoke, not the fire. The fire is gambling that has become an addiction, a debt you’re carrying alone, and thoughts of dying that are coming most nights. I want to deal with all three, starting with keeping you safe.
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives a clear working formulation in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: About the insurance thought — the debt is lying to you. Your partner and your baby need you, not a payout. Forty thousand pounds is a problem that people get through with the right help. Losing you is not.
SCA_MODELS.why: Challenges the ‘better off without me’ belief with compassion

SCA_MODELS.text: It doesn’t feel fixable at three in the morning.

No, and that’s exactly why I don’t want to give you sleeping tablets today. With the drinking and these thoughts, a box of tablets at home is a risk, not a help. Instead, I’d like the mental health crisis team to speak to you today. Would you be okay with me calling them now, while we’re talking?
SCA_MODELS.why: Declines the hypnotic for safety and arranges same-day crisis involvement

SCA_MODELS.text: Today? …Okay. If you think so.

Then there’s the gambling itself. There are free NHS and national services that treat this — group therapy works well. The National Gambling Helpline is open 24 hours and can link you in, and I’ll refer you too. You can also block the betting sites today with GamStop and turn on a gambling block with your bank.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specialist treatment, self-exclusion and blocking made concrete

SCA_MODELS.text: I didn’t know you could block them all.

And the debt: free debt charities negotiate with lenders every day and can often freeze the pressure. Would you be willing to ring one this week? Meanwhile, could we agree the drinking stays down while the crisis team works with you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares decisions on debt advice and alcohol reduction

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah. I can try to cut the drinking.

About your partner — that’s your decision and your timing. Many people find the secret is heavier than the debt. If and when you want to tell her, I or the gambling service can help you plan how, and there’s support for partners too.
SCA_MODELS.why: Supports disclosure at his pace without pressure

SCA_MODELS.text: Let’s write a safety plan together now: what sets the thoughts off, what helps, who you can call. If you ever feel you might act on these thoughts, call 999 or go to A&E, or call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option. I’ll see you again within a couple of days. Does that feel doable?
SCA_MODELS.why: Safety plan, explicit crisis routes and early follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah. It feels a bit less like I’m drowning.
Can you tell me in your own words what happens after this call, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Crisis team rings me today. I call the gambling helpline and block the sites. Debt charity this week. See you in two days. And if it gets bad, 999 or A&E.

SCA_STEM.name: Ryan Doherty
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
No previous mental health contact recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: No consultations on record for sleep or mood. Works as a warehouse team leader. Partner is pregnant.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment booked: “can’t sleep — wants something to help”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG248 (2025) · NICE NG225 (2022) · NICE TA77 · NICE NG222 (2022, updated December 2025) · BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: “Give me something to sleep, I don’t want the why” is a request to look for the why. Here it is gambling harm with concealed debt and suicidal thinking. Ask about gambling and suicide directly, respond to risk the same day, and treat the gambling as a health problem with specialist help.

points.t: NICE TA77: hypnotics only after non-drug measures have been considered, for severe insomnia, and for short periods only. A new hypnotic for a man who is drinking more and thinking about dying adds sedation and a stock of tablets, and treats nothing.

NICE NG248: use a person-centred, empathic and non-judgemental approach, mindful of the shame, fear and stigma of disclosure. Gambling harm hides behind sleep problems, low mood, alcohol and money worries. The PGSI (Problem Gambling Severity Index) scores 0–27; 8 or more suggests the person, or those close to them, are likely experiencing gambling-related harm.

NICE NG248: gambling harm includes suicidal thoughts; ask about them directly. Explore thoughts, plans, intent, preparation (looking at a life-insurance policy counts), access to means, alcohol and protective factors. Asking does not plant the idea.

NICE NG225: do not use risk assessment tools or a low/medium/high label to predict suicide or decide who gets care. Base the response on his needs and what he tells you: hopelessness, debt, shame, alcohol and a preparatory act justify same-day mental health crisis involvement.

NICE NG248: group CBT is the first psychological treatment. NHS specialist gambling services and the National Gambling Support Network take referrals, including self-referral via the National Gambling Helpline (0808 8020 133, 24 hours). Naltrexone is only considered by a specialist if psychological therapy has not worked (off-label).

Blocking and self-exclusion: GamStop (online operators licensed in Great Britain, for 6 months, 1 year or 5 years) and bank gambling blocks. Free debt advice: StepChange, National Debtline, Citizens Advice. Alcohol: AUDIT-C, and the UK CMO low-risk limit of 14 units a week. Screen mood (NICE NG222).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question about the nights; acknowledged the sleep request without prescribing on it; let him explain before narrowing.
Work, pregnant partner, money worries, drinking to sleep, secrecy and shame.
Picked up “I don’t want the why”, “money” and “drinking more”, and explored each gently.
Idea (work stress), concern (the secret debt and his partner finding out), expectation (sleeping tablets, no questions).
Face-to-face review if needed; PHQ-9 and AUDIT-C; PGSI to measure gambling severity; physical health only as indicated.
Primary insomnia vs depression vs anxiety vs alcohol vs gambling harm; tested the stress explanation.
Asked directly about suicidal thoughts, frequency, plan, preparation (life-insurance policy), means, alcohol and protective factors.
Gambling harm with concealed debt, secondary insomnia, increasing alcohol use and suicidal thoughts with a preparatory act, stated plainly.
Declined a hypnotic for safety; same-day crisis team contact; specialist gambling referral; GamStop and bank block; debt advice.
Alcohol reduction agreed; mood screen; partner support offered at his pace.
Written safety plan; 999, A&E and NHS 111 mental health option named; review within two days; risk documented.

social.t: Around £40,000 on cards and loans, hidden from a pregnant partner. Shame and fear of discovery drive the concealment, the drinking and the suicidal thinking; debt advice is part of the treatment, not an add-on.
Exhausted at work as a team leader and drinking most nights to sleep. Alcohol raises impulsivity and suicide risk and worsens sleep.

legal.t: His gambling and debt are confidential, including from his partner (GMC Confidentiality 2017). Disclosure without consent is justified only to prevent a risk of death or serious harm, and involving crisis services here is done with his agreement.
Not a first step. If risk escalated and he refused help, the crisis team would assess whether a Mental Health Act assessment is needed.

The Breathing Space (Debt Respite Scheme) in England and Wales gives legal protection from creditor action; a mental health crisis version exists for people receiving crisis treatment. Debt advisers can apply for it.

professional.t: Declining a hypnotic is good prescribing: NICE TA77 limits hypnotics to short periods after non-drug measures, and tablets are a means of overdose. Explain the reason and offer a better plan (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Record his words about the insurance policy, frequency of thoughts, protective factors, alcohol, the safety plan, who was contacted and when, and the follow-up date.

community.t: National Gambling Helpline 0808 8020 133 (24 hours), National Gambling Support Network and NHS gambling clinics; GamStop self-exclusion; Gamblers Anonymous; support for affected partners and families.
Local crisis team, NHS 111 mental health option, Samaritans (116 123); StepChange, National Debtline and Citizens Advice for free debt advice.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts most nights with a preparatory act (looking at the life-insurance policy) — same-day crisis assessment
Rising alcohol use to sleep — raises impulsivity and overdose risk
Hopelessness and feeling trapped by concealed debt
psychosocial: Gambling: type, frequency, chasing losses, borrowing, secrecy
Debt size and creditors; any pressure from lenders
Pregnant partner who does not know; work performance; alcohol
ice: Idea: “It’s just work stress keeping me awake.”
Concern: the secret debt, his partner finding out, and a sense that his family would be better off with the insurance
Expectation: sleeping tablets and no questions

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Gambling harm (likely gambling disorder) with around £40,000 of concealed debt, secondary insomnia, increasing alcohol use and frequent suicidal thoughts with a preparatory act. Protective factors: his partner and the coming baby.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your sleep problem is the smoke, not the fire. The fire is gambling that has turned into an addiction, a debt you’ve carried alone, and dark thoughts that come most nights. All three are treatable, and we start today.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in wanting to be knocked out so you could stop thinking. I understand why. What I’d like instead is to take away the things you’re lying awake about.”
management.psychosocial: Treat the shame as part of the illness: no judgement, debt advice as a health intervention, and support to tell his partner when he chooses.
sharedPlan: No hypnotic; same-day mental health crisis team contact with his agreement
Specialist gambling referral (NHS service or National Gambling Support Network); GamStop and bank gambling block today
Free debt advice this week; agreed alcohol reduction; mood screen and review
safetyNet: Written safety plan; 999 or A&E if he feels he might act; NHS 111 mental health option; Samaritans 116 123
GP review within two days; risk and plan documented

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by candidates who treat the request (sleeping tablets) instead of the person. The disclosure only happens in a non-judgemental space, and once gambling surfaces the suicide question is mandatory.

items.fail: Prescribing zopiclone for “work stress” after a two-minute sleep history.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice” and unsafe: NICE TA77 limits hypnotics, and tablets are a means of overdose in someone at risk.
items.fix: Say out loud why you want the cause first, then ask what the head is racing about.

items.fail: Asking about stress and work, but never about money, alcohol or gambling.
items.why: The engine of the case stays hidden. NICE NG248 expects gambling to be asked about when the picture fits.
items.fix: “Sometimes it’s money, drinking or betting that’s got out of hand — any of that in the mix?”

items.fail: Hearing about £40,000 of secret debt and moving straight to debt advice without asking about suicide.
items.why: Gambling harm carries a high suicide risk; missing the direct question is a safety fail.
items.fix: “Has it got so heavy you’ve thought your family would be better off without you?” Then plan, preparation, means and protective factors.

items.fail: Reacting to the debt with surprise or a lecture about responsibility.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s emotional cues”; shame shuts him down and he withholds the suicidal thoughts.
items.fix: Thank him, name the courage, and frame gambling as a treatable addiction.

items.fail: Insisting he tells his partner today.
items.why: Pushing disclosure before safety damages trust and can raise risk.
items.fix: Offer help with telling her when he chooses; keep today’s focus on safety and support.

items.fail: Ending with “ring us if you feel worse” and a routine review in a month.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting for a man with frequent suicidal thoughts and a preparatory act is a clear fail.
items.fix: Same-day crisis contact, written safety plan, named routes (999, A&E, NHS 111 mental health option), review within two days, teach-back.
